You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test `testReadingOfFirstStoredEntry` tests reading a ZIP entry from a file "COMPRESS-264.zip" and expects the entry's size to be 5 and content to be "data\n". The current bug report states that commons-compress 1.6 reads the file correctly, but version 1.7 returns NUL bytes in the content, indicating incorrect data reading.

Examining the method `ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry()`, we see that it reads the local file header, sets up the current entry, and prepares an input stream (current.in) to read the entry content. For uncompressed entries (stored method), it likely relies on this input stream to read raw bytes. The method `readFully(byte[])` reads bytes fully from the input stream with `IOUtils.readFully`.

The `readFully` method in `IOUtils` reads bytes using the underlying stream's `read` method until the requested length is obtained or EOF. The method works correctly normally.

A possible fault is in how the entry size or content length is determined or how the input stream is constructed for stored entries in 1.7. The bug report mentions that 1.7 produces NUL bytes, suggesting that the input stream may be empty or zero-filled.

Also, the method `dosToJavaTime` used for setting the entry's modification time contains a subtle bug: it constructs the seconds by shifting `dosTime << 1` which is incorrect; it should mask with bits shifted right, but this bug does not seem connected to the current reading problem.

Focusing on the main symptom: the entry size is read, but the actual bytes returned from the input stream are incorrect, replaced by NUL bytes. This suggests that in 1.7, the stream from which `IOUtils.toByteArray(in)` reads is not correctly providing the stored entry's content bytes.

Comparing the `getNextZipEntry`, we see that the input stream `current.in` is only set for compressed methods (lines 277-284), but for stored (uncompressed) entries, there is no explicit input stream setup - likely it defaults to the main input stream.

It is possible in Commons Compress 1.7 the input stream position after reading the local file header is not correctly set to the start of entry data or the `current.in` stream is not set for stored entries, leading to zero bytes read.

In summary, the root cause is likely related to the treatment of stored entries in `getNextZipEntry()` or the input stream from which entry data is read in 1.7. The test failure and bug report of NUL bytes indicates that `current.in` for stored entries is either not set correctly or the stream is not positioned correctly to read the actual entry data.

No recent bug reports obviously relate to this ZIP reading problem, so this is likely a regression or oversight in 1.7.

Potential fixes involve ensuring that for stored (uncompressed) entries, the input stream `current.in` is correctly wrapped to read exactly the compressed size bytes from the main input stream (possibly a `BoundedInputStream`) starting after the local file header, as was likely done in 1.6.

Thus, the bug occurs because the input stream used for reading stored entry data is not correctly set up in `ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry()`, causing reading of incorrect bytes (NULs), failing the test.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
